**My verdict: the implementation is a credible synthetic feasibility demo, but the report overstates what it establishes.** I independently reran all 18 training runs and three untrained-encoder controls. The useful result survives scrutiny: Q-SIGReg improves the scale and distribution of its four-dimensional projection head. Quantum superiority, reliable Gaussianization, and negligible QPU overhead are not established. 1. **The main numerical pattern reproduces.** My three-seed averages were: | Method | Effective rank | Held-out RBF-MMD² | Energy distance | |---|---:|---:|---:| | No regularizer | 2.54 | 0.6237 | 1.1286 | | Moments | 3.93 | 0.0789 | 0.1166 | | Standard SIGReg | 3.93 | 0.0057 | 0.0363 | | Quantum MMD | 2.93 | 0.0786 | 0.1928 | | Quantum MMD + moments | 3.80 | 0.0537 | 0.1092 | Q-SIGReg improves over no regularization, but SIGReg gives roughly nine times lower RBF discrepancy and three times lower energy distance. Moments alone also recover higher effective rank. The data demonstrate feasibility, not a quantum win. 2. **The downstream accuracy is not evidence of useful self-supervised learning here.** The no-regularizer model gets 100% probe accuracy. More decisively, randomly initialized encoders with zero self-supervised training average **99.35%** across the same three seeds. The probe uses the 32-dimensional backbone, while the distribution metrics use the four-dimensional head. Thus head collapse and a successful backbone probe can coexist. Include this random-encoder control and use a harder task before making downstream claims. 3. **The moment-control comparison is confounded.** Covariance-only computes moments on the full batch every step; Q-SIGReg and the classical RBF variant compute them on eight samples every fourth step. This changes frequency, effective weighting, and finite-sample bias. For iid isotropic Gaussian embeddings with covariance tI, the expected sample-moment penalty alone is minimized at **t = 0.546875 for batch 8**, versus **t ≈ 0.9192 for batch 64**. I derived this and checked it by Monte Carlo. An unbiased sample covariance does not make its squared error unbiased. Also, the variant labeled “Classical RBF-MMD” actually includes moments. Match anchor batch, schedule, and weights; distinguish pure RBF-MMD from RBF-MMD plus moments before attributing differences to the quantum kernel. 4. **The mathematics supports a limited, useful claim.** Fidelity MMD matches average density matrices: MMD² = ||E[rho(Z)] − E[rho(G)]||²_F. A fixed four-qubit map has at most 255 varying real features, so it cannot identify arbitrary continuous distributions; adding ordinary moments does not change that conclusion. It can penalize complete collapse and some higher-order discrepancies. The defensible description is “finite-feature quantum-kernel regularization on four-dimensional embeddings,” not a guaranteed replacement for Gaussian identification. The terminal shared CZ ring cancels in fidelity and can be removed without changing the kernel. 5. **The quantum execution claims need correction.** Training uses exact differentiable PyTorch statevectors, not SamplerQNN or hardware. The 1,296 count is forward pair-kernel evaluations per run; it omits Qiskit parameter-shift circuit evaluations and shots. The timings measure simulator training, excluding evaluation and probing. Our earlier direct Qiskit check required 49 forward/backward bindings per pair in the naïve implementation. A fixed circuit avoids optimizing quantum weights, but does not eliminate input-gradient cost or guarantee against vanishing gradients. Neither the “90% classical / 10% quantum” split nor “negligible QPU overhead” was measured. The shot-budget statement is also too strong. One estimated probability has standard error sqrt(p(1−p)/N), at most 0.044 at 128 shots and 0.005 at 10,000. Those are not guarantees of detecting a distribution difference. More shots do not remove the large paired-estimator sampling noise at batch 8, systematic hardware errors, or uncertainty in combined gradients. Diagonal kernel normalization alone does not guarantee a valid PSD kernel or repair all noise effects. 6. **Collapse and verification claims need tighter wording.** The implementation reports effective rank 4 even for an exactly zero covariance matrix because it floors every eigenvalue before normalization. Its “Complete Collapse” initialization is actually nonzero Gaussian noise with standard deviation 0.01. Report absolute variance and minimum eigenvalue alongside rank, and distinguish near-collapse from exact collapse. The results remain useful, but “fully restores dimensionality” needs those additional checks.
